While models intended for policy evaluation are generally simpler than those used for contact tracing, neither category constitutes a definitive limit; for instance, traced epidemics have been managed using basic compartmental approaches. Furthermore, models designed for specific tasks, such as forecasting infection counts or assessing measures, are not inherently superior to those meant for other goals like estimating basic reproduction numbers ($R_0$) or heterogeneities (e.g., via phylogenetic analysis). Consequently, it is erroneous to claim that forecasts imply a lack of knowledge regarding $R_0$ or that such metrics are obsolete. Finally, models focused on contact tracing must explicitly incorporate the relevant mechanisms, whether this involves mechanistic descriptions of apps and protocols or the mathematical formulation of how tracing alters reproduction numbers. Building on this, we propose a framework capable of incorporating any 3D transformation, including rotations, translations, and non-isometric changes like scaling and shearing. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses existing techniques, achieving significant improvements in downstream tasks such as classification and retrieval. Furthermore, the framework exhibits consistent gains across various point cloud representations, 3D transformations, and downstream applications, even optimizing the performance of counter-intuitive combinations. These findings underscore the transformation and representation-dependent nature of our approach. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ahadadami/Neighborhood_tpc.

Conversely, our proposed Geometric Proof Method (GPM) for program optimization utilizes a bottom-up strategy where equality rules are applied implicitly. By employing this geometric approach, we can concisely demonstrate the correctness of equality rules within program transformation rules, thereby establishing them as reasoning rules. Situational multi-armed bandits (sMB) model advertisements, products, or actions presented to users within specific contexts, such as their location or current activity. In this setup, a manufacturer aims to maximize revenue by selecting the optimal item for each context, under the assumption that availability within any given context follows a long-tailed distribution where only a limited number of high-value items are present. Previous learning algorithms for sMB were developed in centralized frameworks, which demand significant computational resources and introduce single points of failure. This research investigates on-line learning within a distributed sMB framework to determine the optimal rate for maximizing revenue in dynamic contexts. The authors first introduce two new metrics to quantify information access limits among agents due to restricted context visibility and item availability. They then propose a novel on-line algorithm that achieves the best possible revenue maximization rate, accounting for both item availability and information access constraints. Notably, this algorithm requires no prior knowledge regarding the distribution of contexts, items, or revenue per item. Finally, the algorithm is implemented and tested using a real-world dataset from Weibo, a Chinese micro-blogging platform.

The external layers of protoplanetary disks are active sites for complex chemical processes, including the formation and settling of dust. While recent hydrodynamical simulations demonstrated that the instability responsible for spinning up giant gas giants (vertical shear instability [VSI]) is suppressed by dust, those models utilized simplified "gray" diffusion frameworks that lack physical realism in the outer regions ($\gtrsim 3$ AU) of typical protoplanetary disks. In these areas, dust accumulation likely triggers radiative trapping and creates localized dust clouds within an otherwise clear gas environment. This study investigates how dust cloud formation specifically influences VSI growth rates in the outer regions of standard protoplanetary disks. We developed a new simulation framework where dust cloud formation and subsequent clearing are coupled with VSI flow evolution. The results indicate that initial dust settling suppresses VSI amplification of vertical velocity perturbations by approximately an order of magnitude. Furthermore, dust cloud formation causes VSI-driven vortices to confine clouds at their centers rather than continuing to expand. Notably, when dust clearing is coupled with the instability, vortices grow larger as if unaffected by dust, though this expansion is accompanied by intermittent accretion-driven bursts. Ultimately, a combination of dust cloud formation, settling, and horizontal migration offers a plausible mechanism for generating large-scale vortices in the external regions of typical protoplanetary disks. To examine this mechanism within a realistic context, we modeled the PIA 223-11 region of the Class 0 protostar B325 using a self-consistent approach that incorporates dust cloud formation, opening, and recurrence alongside VSI dynamics. These simulations successfully produced large vortices in the outer regions ($\gtrsim 3$ AU) of B325, consistent with observed gas density enhancements, all while remaining aligned with constraints on total mass and vertical velocity derived from fall-back accretion rates. We conclude that future observations of dust density enhancements in the external regions of protoplanetary disks can help refine models of this mechanism, potentially serving as an indirect method to detect VSI activity in such regions. Additionally, a version of this mechanism could operate in the outer regions of the disks around young gas giants, potentially enabling them to acquire the large vertical velocity perturbations necessary for their formation. This paper introduces two techniques to enhance the classification of static images: dynamic entrances and global mean pooling. Although these methods appear trivial, they yield substantial improvements without adding significant computational cost. With dynamic entrances, a fully connected layer is substituted by a segmentaion module that initially applies average pooling and subsequently selects specific segments for further processing. For the global mean pooling module, the segmentation module is omitted, and only the globally averaged features are forwarded. Experiments conducted on the MNIST, EMNIST-byrow, EMNIST-palette, and USPS datasets demonstrate that even the simplest neural network architectures can achieve near-perfect classification accuracy with both modules integrated. Furthermore, testing on the CIFAR-10 dataset reveals that these modules can significantly boost performance, resulting in a 1.08% reduction in misclassification rate with a single segmentation module and an additional 0.5% improvement with two modules. With both modules implemented, the best-reported accuracy of 99.06% was attained. Finally, the impact of the position of the segmentation module on classification accuracy was also evaluated. Neither the global average pooling nor the dynamic segmentation module should be the first averaging operation within the network; as evidenced by our experiments, prior averaging modules do not yield positive results. Ultimately, this work highlights that the segmentation module is actually a "class mean segmentation" mechanism, which has been utilized in mean segmentation based layers for class activation mapping [1] and external segmentation modules for attention mechanisms [2, 3].

This work addresses the challenge of Federated Learning (FL) across heterogeneous data distributions, where data providers refuse to categorize their inputs, creating distinct and potentially non-convex distribution shifts. Traditional strategies, such as those based on Meta Gradient Descent, demand access to support vectors from each provider, a requirement often unmet in practical scenarios. Furthermore, methods relying on multiple global model updates per local update risk excessive computation and communication costs. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Random Stroll (RS), a novel approach that requires no prior knowledge of data distributions and operates without second-order information or support vectors. RS functions by iteratively adjusting model parameters in random directions at each local update step. Empirical results from both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that RS effectively trains a global model capable of classifying out-ofdistribution data. Additionally, we conducted extensive comparisons against state-of-the-art techniques using the MNIST, EMNIST, and MNAC datasets. These experiments confirm that RS achieves performance comparable to other methods on in-distribution data while successfully handling out-of-distribution inputs where alternatives fail. Finally, the experiments highlight RS's advantage in accelerating convergence from non-convex data distributions. We open-source our code at https://github.com/Mohamed-Ahmed-Mohie/Random-Stroll-FL. Keywords: Federated Learning, Heterogeneous Data, Random Stroll, Convergence Rate, Out-of-Distribution Data.

We present a theoretical examination of nonlocal phenomena arising from single-particle entanglement in quantum systems. We demonstrate that Bohmian nonlocality, a form of nonlocal guidance between simultaneously detected particles, stems directly from the nonlocality of the vacuum and aligns with a causal, local, deterministic, and realist model of single-particle dynamics. We highlight that nonlocal single-particle effects, which have been observed, represent a distinct, weaker form of nonlocality characterized by statistical correlations rather than deterministic correlations. Finally, we outline how both the nonlocality of single-particle dynamics and its associated correlations can be harnessed to establish secure quantum cryptography based on single-particle correlations. These findings clarify the origins of different nonlocal effects in single-particle phenomena and underscore that neither entanglement nor many-particle systems are required to produce nonlocal outcomes. We conclude by addressing the implications of these results for various interpretations of quantum mechanics, particularly local hidden variable theories, causal models, and theories unifying quantum mechanics with general relativity. These nonlocal single-particle effects serve as a significant obstacle for local causal hidden variable models, local causal realist models, and local realist models of metric gravity, as well as for Bohmian mechanics, which relies on nonlocal particle guidance. Additionally, these effects challenge the principle of metric gravity's locality, even in the absence of many-particle interactions. These conclusions are illustrated with concrete examples throughout this work, which avoids reliance on controversial assumptions found in other approaches to this topic. The arguments presented here complement those in other recent studies examining nonlocality in single-particle quantum phenomena [1–12]. This study introduces a hardware-friendly model without sacrificing accuracy, suitable for real-time video analysis on constrainted embedded systems. We introduce a fully customized tensor-hardware architecture and a corresponding LSTM network structure tailored for specific video recognition tasks. By leveraging the low-rank characteristics of 3D tensors from real videos, we propose a hierarchical Tucker (HT) decomposition to compress the network's weight matrix. This compression enables further hardware optimizations during both compilation and runtime. With these "software-defined" hardware co-design strategies, an HT-labeled LSTM network achieves a 10x reduction in adder tree area and a 20x decrease in weight memory footprint compared to conventional fully connected layers. Alignment gains from HT-decomposition further accelerate inference without extra cost. Consequently, our specialized LSTM architecture delivers a 3x faster inference rate than the standard layer structure, utilizing identical adder resources and weight memory. Finally, we demonstrate that this approach supports real-time processing for CMe-1 and Senseable datasets: 19x and 10x real-time performance on CMe-1, and 7.8x real-time performance on Senseable, using an ultra-low power FPGA (XC7A35T). The proposed method is universally applicable to any video identifier, particularly benefiting low-resource scenarios. The accompanying open-source code and model are accessible at: https://github.com/TianweiT/HT-LSTM. These materials support this work and will receive the award. (This article won the Best Paper Award at DAC 2019).
